Empirical Research Plan  
“Does a multi-faceted Graduation‐style program raise the long-run income and well-being of the ultra-poor across six countries?”

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Method: Difference-in-Differences (DID) embedded in a multi-site randomized controlled trial (RCT).

Rationale  
• Random assignment of households or villages to “Graduation” vs. “Control” gives internal validity.  
• Two (sometimes three) survey waves (baseline t0, short-run t1, long-run t2) allow us to difference out time-invariant unobservables and absorb common macro shocks.  
• Pooling six country-level experiments in a single DID (with site fixed effects and site-specific time trends) delivers:  
 (a) one overall average treatment effect (ATE) and  
 (b) site-specific ATEs for external‐validity comparisons.  

Optional extensions  
• Event-study graph (baseline, midline, endline) to visualize dynamics.  
• Instrumental-Variables (IV) for treatment take-up, using random assignment as the instrument, when compliance is imperfect.  

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable  
T_i = 1 if household i (or its village) was randomly assigned to receive the full Graduation package; 0 otherwise.

Control group  
Non-treated households in the same randomization strata (village or household-level randomization). They receive “status-quo” services only.

Timing  
Post_t = 1 for surveys conducted after the 24-36-month program ends (main endline); 0 for baseline. A second post dummy (Mid_t) marks the 1-year survey for event-study plots.

Randomization strata  
Strata_s are country-site × randomization wave × (if applicable) village-pair cells. All regressions include these fixed effects.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Randomization ⇒ Parallel Trends in expectation.  
Because treatment was randomly assigned prior to baseline data collection, average outcome paths of treated and control households would have been identical absent the program.

A2. Stable Unit Treatment Value (SUTVA).  
No spillovers or interference from treated to control households within the sample frame, and no variant of treatment beyond the defined package.

A3. Stable Composition.  
Attrition or sample replacement is not systematically different across treatment arms nor correlated with potential outcomes.

Plausibility  
• A1 is highly plausible given the RCT design; we will still test it by verifying balanced pre-treatment covariates and parallel pre-trends where midline precedes most income gains.  
• A2 is more delicate—physical asset transfers (livestock) or coaching could spill over within villages; village-level randomization in several sites is intended to minimize such within-community spillovers.  
• A3 will be checked using attrition tables and Lee bounds.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Main Threats and Mitigations
--------------------------------------------------------------------
T1. Differential Attrition  
  Mitigation: (i) compare attrition rates and baseline characteristics by arm; (ii) re-weight observations using inverse-probability weights; (iii) Lee bounds on ATEs.

T2. Spillovers / General-Equilibrium Effects  
  Mitigation: cluster randomization where possible; include buffer zones; measure control-group exposure to treated neighbors; run sensitivity checks omitting high-density areas.

T3. Implementation Heterogeneity and Non-Compliance  
  Mitigation: conduct ITT as main specification; TOT via two-stage least squares with random assignment as instrument for actual receipt; include site × treatment interactions; document program fidelity metrics.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
--------------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# 0. Packages
library(data.table)   # fast data handling
library(fixest)       # high-dim FE regressions
library(estimatr)     # randomization inference, if desired
library(ggplot2)

# 1. Data Loading
dat  <- fread("graduation_six_country_panel.csv")  # stacked country panels
# key variables assumed in file: hhid, country, strata, village, wave (0=B,1=M,2=E),
# treat_assign, outcome_cons_pc, weight, etc.

# 2. Variable Construction
dat[, post  := as.integer(wave == 2)]       # Endline dummy
dat[, mid   := as.integer(wave == 1)]       # Midline dummy
dat[, treat := treat_assign]                # ITT

# 3. Main DID Specification (ANCOVA preferred)
did_main <- feols(outcome_cons_pc_endline ~ treat + outcome_cons_pc_baseline
                  | country + strata,          # FE absorb design strata
                  weights = ~weight,
                  cluster = ~village,          # cluster at randomization level
                  data = dat[wave == 2])       # endline only for ANCOVA
summary(did_main)

# Alternative two-way DID with both periods
did_tw   <- feols(outcome_cons_pc ~ treat*post | strata + hhid,
                  cluster = ~village,
                  weights = ~weight,
                  data = dat[wave %in% c(0,2)])
summary(did_tw)

# 4. Event Study (Baseline, Midline, Endline)
dat[, wave_f := factor(wave)]
es <- feols(outcome_cons_pc ~ i(wave_f, treat, ref=0) | strata + hhid,
            cluster = "village", data = dat)
iplot(es) + theme_bw()

# 5. Robustness Check: Lee Bounds for Attrition
# illustration for consumption outcome
source("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ladyzenith/leeBounds/master/R/leeBounds.R")
lb <- leeBounds(y="outcome_cons_pc", D="treat", attr="attrited", 
                data=dat[wave==2], alpha=.05)
print(lb)
```

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Direction: Positive. The bundle of asset transfer + training + regular coaching + consumption smoothing should raise consumption, income, savings, and psychological well-being, and reduce food insecurity.

Magnitude (based on BRAC Bangladesh and prior pilots):  
• Per-capita consumption: +0.10 to +0.20 log points (~10-22 %).  
• Household asset index: +0.25–0.40 SD.  
• Food security (share of days with adequate meals): +5-10 pp.  
• Psychological well-being: +0.15–0.25 SD.

We expect most gains to persist (or grow) between t1 and t2, consistent with a move to a higher income trajectory rather than a one-off windfall.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DID / RCT)
--------------------------------------------------------------------
C1. Successful random assignment (balance at baseline) ............... 1  
C2. No interference / spillovers (SUTVA) ............................. 0.5  
C3. Low and balanced attrition ....................................... 0.5  
C4. Accurate, consistent outcome measurement across waves ............ 1  
C5. Correct functional form / proper SE clustering ................... 1  

Total (out of 5): 4.0  
Items with partial scores (C2, C3) will be scrutinized in robustness analyses described above.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
This plan leverages the strong internal validity of the multi-site RCT, formalizes the DID framework for estimation, anticipates major threats, and provides reproducible code for core analyses and robustness checks.
